Re: First Amendment to the Amended & Restated Limited Partnership Agreement of Driftwood Absolute Return Fund Ltd. (Cayman Registration No. ELP-87234) — Response to IAC Counsel Comments

I write on behalf of Calderwood & Harkness LLP, counsel to Driftwood Capital Management LLC ("DCM" or the "General Partner"), the general partner of Driftwood Absolute Return Fund Ltd. ("DARF" or the "Fund"), in response to the detailed written comments submitted by Wexford Crane & Albright LLP ("WCA"), dated July 31, 2024, on the draft First Amendment (the "First Amendment") to the Amended & Restated Limited Partnership Agreement of DARF, dated as of March 15, 2017 (the "A&R LPA").

As you are aware, the draft First Amendment was circulated to all forty-seven (47) limited partners of the Fund on July 15, 2024, together with the Successor Key Person Proposal and the Form of LP Written Consent. The circulation was undertaken in accordance with the notice and consent solicitation procedures set forth in Section 14.01 of the A&R LPA.

We wish to express our appreciation for the thoughtful and constructive engagement of WCA and the members of the Investor Advisory Committee (the "IAC") throughout this process. In particular, the productive discussion that took place at the IAC meeting held on July 29, 2024, was extremely helpful in focusing the areas of agreement and identifying the limited points requiring further clarification. As you know, that meeting was chaired by Diana Cortland of the Northvale Public Employees' Retirement System and attended by IAC members Richard Oshima (Sycamore Endowment Partners LP), Catherine Mercer (Velthorn Institutional Fund of Funds III, L.P.), Thomas Ashworth (Bridlewood Family Office Holdings Ltd.), and Nadia Al-Rashid (Atlas Sovereign Wealth Advisory LLC). Their active participation and candid feedback have been invaluable in shaping the revisions discussed herein.

The purpose of this letter is threefold: (a) to address each of the comments raised by WCA in its July 31 comment letter; (b) to confirm the areas in which the General Partner and the IAC (through its counsel) have reached agreement; and (c) to identify any outstanding points that require further discussion or the circulation of specific drafting language.

We are mindful of the timeline that governs this process. The LP Consent Deadline is August 23, 2024, which represents forty (40) calendar days from the July 15, 2024 circulation date, as provided in the consent solicitation notice. Additionally, the ninety (90)-calendar-day Cure Period triggered by the Key Person Event expires on September 8, 2024, pursuant to Section 8.04(b) of the A&R LPA. Both of these deadlines underscore the importance of achieving timely resolution of the outstanding matters so that the consent solicitation can proceed on schedule and the governance transition can be effectuated within the contractual framework.

For the avoidance of doubt, the relevant factual context is as follows. The Key Person Event was triggered on June 10, 2024, following the medical incapacitation of Marcus J. Whitmore, the Fund's founder, Chief Investment Officer, and sole Key Person under Section 8.04(a) of the A&R LPA. Mr. Whitmore suffered a hemorrhagic stroke on June 3, 2024, and was determined by his attending physicians to be unable to resume his duties as CIO for an indefinite period, constituting a "Disability" under Section 1.01(dd) of the A&R LPA. Written notification of the Key Person Event was delivered by the General Partner to all limited partners on June 14, 2024, which was within the five (5)-business-day contractual notification deadline of June 17, 2024, as required by Section 8.04(b). As a consequence of the Key Person Event, the Investment Period is currently suspended and follow-on investments are capped at $28.7 million, representing 1.0% of assets under management ("AUM"), in accordance with Section 8.04(c)(ii).

We are pleased to confirm that, as discussed at the July 29 IAC meeting and reflected in WCA's comment letter, there is no objection from the IAC to the designation of Elaine R. Sato and Jonathan K. Huang as joint Successor Key Persons under the proposed amended Section 8.04(a) of the A&R LPA.

The designation of the Successor Key Persons requires the affirmative written consent of limited partners holding not less than 66⅔% of aggregate limited partner capital commitments (excluding the General Partner's co-investment), as set forth in Section 14.01(b)(iii) of the A&R LPA. The voting threshold is accordingly $1,865.50 million of the $2,798.25 million in voting limited partner commitments. Based on the feedback received from the IAC members at the July 29 meeting, as well as informal indications received from several additional limited partners, the General Partner is optimistic that this consent threshold will be comfortably achieved within the August 23, 2024 deadline.

WCA has requested that during the 180-day Replacement Period, any proposed replacement Successor Key Person be subject to consultation with the IAC (though not a formal veto right) prior to the General Partner's circulation of a replacement proposal to the limited partners for consent.

GP Response: The General Partner agrees with this comment in principle. The revised draft will provide that, prior to circulating any proposed replacement of a lost Successor Key Person to the limited partners for consent under Section 14.01, the General Partner shall consult with the IAC in good faith regarding the qualifications, experience, and suitability of the proposed replacement candidate. Such consultation shall include, at a minimum, the delivery of the proposed replacement candidate's curriculum vitae, a summary of his or her relevant experience, and the proposed terms of his or her economic participation in the General Partner, in each case not less than ten (10) business days prior to the circulation of the replacement proposal to the limited partners.

It is understood and agreed, however, that the IAC's role in this process is consultative and advisory in nature and does not constitute a consent right, veto right, or approval right separate from, or in addition to, the ≥ 66⅔% limited partner consent mechanism set forth in Section 14.01(b)(iii) of the A&R LPA. The governance structure of the Fund is predicated on the limited partners exercising their consent rights directly, and the IAC consultation process is intended to facilitate informed decision-making by the limited partner base rather than to create an additional layer of governance authority. We believe this approach appropriately balances the IAC's legitimate interest in being consulted on key personnel decisions with the fundamental consent architecture of the A&R LPA.

WCA has requested that, if both Successor Key Persons are simultaneously lost or if the remaining Successor Key Person is lost during a Single Key Person Period, the consequences shall mirror those set forth in the original Section 8.04(c) of the A&R LPA — namely, immediate suspension of the Investment Period, commencement of a ninety (90)-calendar-day Cure Period, and potential Fund wind-down if the Cure Period expires without resolution.

GP Response: The General Partner agrees. This was always the intended framework, and we appreciate the IAC's request for explicit language to remove any ambiguity. The revised draft will include express language providing that, upon the loss of both Successor Key Persons (whether simultaneously or sequentially, including as a result of the loss of the sole remaining Successor Key Person during a Single Key Person Period), the consequences set forth in Section 8.04(c) of the A&R LPA shall apply in full, including: (i) immediate suspension of the Investment Period; (ii) commencement of a ninety (90)-calendar-day Cure Period; (iii) limitation of new and follow-on investments during the Cure Period as provided therein; and (iv) the right of limited partners holding not less than 66⅔% of aggregate capital commitments to direct the dissolution and winding-up of the Fund if the Cure Period expires without the designation and approval of a new Key Person. This language will be added to amended Section 8.04(e) for the avoidance of doubt.

We acknowledge WCA's comments regarding the scope and authority of the three-member Investment Committee proposed to be established under new Section 8.05 of the A&R LPA. As set forth in the draft First Amendment, the Investment Committee would be composed of Ms. Sato (as Chair), Mr. Huang, and one independent member to be designated by the IAC.

We acknowledge WCA's comment supporting the proposed reduction of the follow-on investment cap during any future Key Person Event from 1.0% of AUM to 0.5% of AUM. The existing 1.0% cap, which currently limits follow-on investments to $28.7 million during the present Key Person Event, was viewed by several IAC members at the July 29 meeting as unduly generous for periods of governance uncertainty.
(a) The aggregate incentive allocation payable by the Fund to the General Partner remains at 20% of net profits above the hurdle rate, as set forth in Section 5.02(b) of the A&R LPA;

(b) The annual management fee remains at 2.0% of committed capital during the Investment Period and 2.0% of invested capital (at cost) following the expiration or suspension of the Investment Period, as set forth in Section 5.01 of the A&R LPA;

(c) The 6% annualized hurdle rate with full catch-up (i.e., 100% of profits between 6% and 7.5% to the General Partner until equalized at a 20/80 split) is unchanged, as set forth in Section 5.02(b)(ii) of the A&R LPA; and
(d) The high-water mark of $142.67 per unit, established as of December 31, 2023, continues in effect, as set forth in Section 5.02(c) of the A&R LPA.

(d) Acceleration. For the avoidance of doubt, all unvested carried interest shall vest in full upon the earliest to occur of (i) Mr. Whitmore's death; (ii) a dissolution and winding-up of the Fund; or (iii) a Change of Control of the General Partner, as defined in Section 1.01(p) of the A&R LPA.

GP Response: The General Partner agrees to the inclusion of such a statement. The General Partner acknowledges that its fiduciary obligations under the Delaware Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act, 6 Del. C. § 17-101 et seq., and under the A&R LPA, including but not limited to the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing and the duties of loyalty and care to the extent not modified by the A&R LPA, are not diminished, suspended, modified, or waived during a Key Person Event, a Replacement Period, or a Single Key Person Period. The First Amendment will include a confirming statement to this effect.

The General Partner notes, however, that the existing exculpation and indemnification provisions of the A&R LPA — specifically, Section 10.01 (Exculpation) and Section 10.02 (Indemnification) — remain in full force and effect and are not modified by the First Amendment. The inclusion of the fiduciary duty acknowledgment is not intended to, and shall not be construed to, alter the standard of liability applicable to the General Partner or its members under Sections 10.01 and 10.02.

For ease of reference, we summarize below the revisions that have been agreed between the General Partner and the IAC (through its counsel) and that will be incorporated into the revised draft of the First Amendment:

2.  IAC Consultation on Replacement Candidates. Non-binding, good faith consultation with the IAC regarding any proposed replacement Successor Key Person prior to circulation to the limited partners for consent.

### documents/matters/1024-00002/Correspondence/lp-notification-letter-key-person-event.docx

Driftwood Capital Management LLC ("DCM"), a Delaware limited liability company, in its capacity as General Partner of Driftwood Absolute Return Fund Ltd. ("DARF" or the "Fund"), a Cayman Islands exempted limited partnership registered with the Registrar of Exempted Limited Partnerships under Registration No. ELP-87234, is writing to you pursuant to the notification obligation set forth in Section 8.04(c) of the Amended & Restated Limited Partnership Agreement of the Fund, dated March 15, 2017 (the "A&R LPA"). The A&R LPA is governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the State of Delaware.

The purpose of this notice is to formally notify all forty-seven (47) limited partners of the Fund (collectively, the "Limited Partners," and each, a "Limited Partner") that a Key Person Event, as that term is defined in Section 8.04(b) of the A&R LPA, has occurred. This notice sets forth the circumstances giving rise to the Key Person Event, the consequences thereof under the A&R LPA, the applicable cure mechanics, the General Partner's intended next steps, and relevant contact information for inquiries. We urge each Limited Partner to review this notice carefully and in its entirety and to consult with its own legal and financial advisors as it deems appropriate.

Section 8.04(a) of the A&R LPA designates Marcus J. Whitmore as the sole "Key Person" of the Fund. Mr. Whitmore is the Founder, Chief Investment Officer, and Managing Member of DCM, holding a ninety percent (90%) ownership interest in DCM. Mr. Whitmore has served continuously as the Key Person of the Fund since the Fund's inception on March 15, 2017. In that capacity, Mr. Whitmore has been principally responsible for the formulation and execution of the Fund's investment strategy, the allocation of capital across the Fund's multi-strategy mandate, and the overall management and direction of the Fund's affairs. His designation as the sole Key Person under the A&R LPA reflects the central and irreplaceable role that Mr. Whitmore has played in the investment management of the Fund since its founding.

The General Partner has been in regular communication with Mr. Whitmore's family members and medical team and will continue to monitor his condition closely. Out of respect for Mr. Whitmore's privacy, the General Partner will not disclose additional details of his medical condition beyond what is necessary to fulfill its obligations under the A&R LPA.

Section 8.04(b) of the A&R LPA provides, in relevant part, that a Key Person Event shall be deemed to have occurred if the Key Person is "unable to devote substantially all of his professional time to the affairs of the Partnership for a period of seven (7) consecutive calendar days" and such absence is not the subject of prior written notice to the Limited Partners.

The occurrence of a Key Person Event triggers a number of material consequences under the A&R LPA, each of which is described below. The General Partner has taken, and will continue to take, all steps necessary to ensure compliance with the provisions of Section 8.04(c) and related sections of the A&R LPA.

Pursuant to Section 8.04(c) of the A&R LPA, the Investment Period of the Fund is immediately suspended as of the Key Person Event Date. The suspension of the Investment Period took effect automatically upon the occurrence of the Key Person Event on June 10, 2024, and no further action by the General Partner or the Limited Partners was required to effectuate such suspension.

During the suspension of the Investment Period, the A&R LPA permits the General Partner to make follow-on investments in existing portfolio positions, subject to a quantitative cap. Specifically, Section 8.04(c) provides that follow-on investments shall not exceed 1.0% of the Fund's assets under management as of the most recently completed calendar month prior to the Key Person Event Date.

The General Partner will track and report all follow-on investments made during the suspension period and will not exceed the Follow-On Cap without the prior written consent of Limited Partners holding at least 66⅔% of the aggregate limited partner capital commitments, as required by the A&R LPA.

•  "Commitment Period" (synonymous with "Investment Period") means the period beginning on the date of the Final Close and ending on the fourth anniversary thereof, during which the General Partner may make new Investments on behalf of the Fund. The Commitment Period is subject to early termination upon a Key Person Event as described in Section VIII.

The LPA establishes a Fund term of ten (10) years commencing on the date of the Final Close. Assuming the Final Close occurs on October 31, 2024 (the stated deadline), the initial term of the Fund would expire on October 31, 2034.

The LPA further provides for two (2) one-year extension periods, each at the sole discretion of the General Partner, which would extend the Fund term to a maximum of twelve (12) years from the Final Close (i.e., potentially through October 31, 2036). Critically, the LPA does not require Limited Partner consent, LPAC approval, or any form of investor vote for either extension period. The GP may exercise each extension unilaterally by providing written notice to the Limited Partners at least 90 days prior to the expiration of the then-current term.

We note that the absence of any LP consent requirement for the extension periods is a less favorable term from BFO's perspective. While the first one-year extension at GP discretion is consistent with common market practice, there is an increasing trend in the institutional private equity market to require some form of investor consent for the second extension year — typically either (i) approval by the Limited Partner Advisory Committee ("LPAC"), or (ii) a vote of a majority or super-majority of Limited Partners. The rationale for such a requirement is that a second extension indicates potential difficulty in realizing the Fund's remaining portfolio, and LPs should have a voice in determining whether continued management by the GP is in the best interests of the Fund.

Recommendation: We recommend that BFO negotiate a side-letter provision requiring LPAC consent or, alternatively, the affirmative vote of Limited Partners holding a super-majority (66⅔% or 75%) of the aggregate Capital Commitments for the exercise of the second one-year extension. If LPAC consent is the mechanism employed, BFO should ensure it has adequate representation on or access to the LPAC, which is discussed further in Section XI.A below.

The LPA includes an interest equalization mechanism for Limited Partners admitted at subsequent closings after the first close. Under this mechanism, subsequent-close LPs are required to contribute their pro rata share of all capital that has previously been called from first-close LPs, together with interest thereon at a rate equal to the Prime Rate plus 2.0% per annum, calculated from the date of each prior capital call through the date of the subsequent-close LP's admission. This interest equalization payment is intended to put subsequent-close LPs in the same economic position as if they had been admitted at the first close. The interest equalization payments are distributed to first-close LPs (and any previously-admitted subsequent-close LPs) in proportion to their respective shares of the prior capital calls. This is a standard provision and does not raise any concerns. Given that BFO is likely to be admitted at or near the first close, we do not anticipate significant interest equalization payments by BFO, though this should be confirmed during the subscription process.

GP Clawback Obligation. The LPA includes a GP clawback provision (Section 7.6 of the LPA), which requires the General Partner to return to the Fund, upon liquidation, any carried interest distributions that, in the aggregate, exceed the amount to which the GP would have been entitled based on the final cumulative performance of the Fund. The clawback obligation is secured by an escrow arrangement pursuant to which 25% of all carried interest distributions received by the GP are deposited into a third-party escrow account and held until the earlier of (i) the final liquidation of the Fund or (ii) the date on which the GP can demonstrate that no clawback obligation remains outstanding. The escrow account is maintained by a third-party escrow agent designated by the GP, and the LPA specifies that the escrow funds may be invested in U.S. Treasury obligations or money market funds pending release.

We draw BFO's particular attention to the broken-deal costs provision. The LPA allocates broken-deal costs to the Fund without any cap or limitation. In an active investment environment where the GP is pursuing multiple opportunities simultaneously, broken-deal costs can be substantial — it is not uncommon for a single failed acquisition to generate $500,000 or more in abort costs (including legal fees, environmental reports, engineering studies, and appraisal fees). Over the life of the Fund, aggregate broken-deal costs could be significant, particularly given Fund IV's strategy of pursuing value-add and opportunistic investments in commercial real estate, which often involves competitive auction processes with high due diligence expenses.

The Investment Period (referred to in the LPA as the "Commitment Period") commences on the date of the Final Close and continues for a period of four (4) years. Assuming the Final Close occurs on October 31, 2024, the Investment Period would expire on October 31, 2028. During the Investment Period, the GP has broad authority to deploy the Fund's capital in new investments in accordance with the Fund's investment strategy and subject to the investment restrictions described below.

The LPA also permits the GP to enter into subscription credit facilities (also known as capital call facilities or subscription lines of credit) secured by the unfunded Capital Commitments of the Limited Partners. The subscription facility is capped at 25% of aggregate unfunded Capital Commitments, with a maximum outstanding term of 180 days (approximately six months). Subscription facilities are commonly used to bridge the timing gap between investment execution and capital call funding, and they can also be used to fund management fees, organizational expenses, and other Fund Expenses. While subscription facilities provide operational flexibility, BFO should be aware that the use of such facilities can have the effect of enhancing reported IRR by delaying capital calls (thereby reducing the period over which LP capital is deemed invested), even though the total dollar return to LPs is unchanged. BFO should consider requesting additional disclosure regarding the Fund's use of subscription facilities in its quarterly reporting.

(a) Cannabis-Related Assets. The LPA does not contain any restriction on investments in real estate assets that are leased to or used in connection with cannabis cultivation, processing, or distribution operations. While cannabis operations are legal under the laws of certain U.S. states, they remain illegal under federal law (the Controlled Substances Act), and investments in cannabis-related real estate present significant legal, regulatory, reputational, and banking risks.

(c) Sanctioned Jurisdictions. While the LPA contains standard OFAC compliance representations, it does not expressly restrict investments in jurisdictions subject to U.S. sanctions or involving parties on the OFAC Specially Designated Nationals List. Given that the Fund's geographic mandate is limited to North America, this is a lower risk, but not zero risk.

The base LPA does not include a general excuse or exclusion right for Limited Partners. This is a significant gap in the LPA from BFO's perspective. In the absence of an excuse right, BFO would be obligated to fund its pro rata share of every capital call issued by the GP during the Investment Period, regardless of the nature of the underlying investment and regardless of any legal, regulatory, or reputational concerns that BFO may have with respect to such investment.

(b) During the Key Person Suspension Period, the GP may propose one or more replacement key persons for approval by the LPAC. The GP must provide the LPAC with a written proposal identifying the proposed replacement, including a description of the proposed replacement's qualifications, experience, and intended role. The LPAC may approve or reject the proposed replacement in its sole discretion.
(c) If the LPAC approves a replacement key person within the 180-day Suspension Period, the Investment Period resumes and continues for its remaining duration as if no Key Person Event had occurred.

(d) If no replacement key person is approved by the LPAC within the 180-day Suspension Period, the Investment Period terminates permanently, and the GP may not make any further new investments on behalf of the Fund.

(c) This individualized suspension right would operate independently of the LPAC process described in the base LPA. That is, even if the LPAC approves a replacement key person and the Fund-level Investment Period resumes, BFO would retain the right to have elected not to participate in future new investments.

This enhanced key person provision is a stronger right than the LPA baseline, which only provides for a Fund-level suspension and requires LPAC action. The individualized suspension right gives BFO direct control over its commitment in the event of a Key Person Event, without requiring BFO to rely on the LPAC (on which BFO may not have a seat, as discussed in Section XI.A below).

We anticipate that the GP may push back on the concept of an individualized suspension right, as it could create disparate treatment among LPs and potentially reduce the Fund's available capital during a critical transitional period. We recommend discussing fallback positions with BFO during the strategy call scheduled for February 5, 2024. Potential fallback positions include: (i) accepting the 180-day suspension period (rather than 90 days) but retaining BFO's unilateral election right; (ii) limiting BFO's election to a right to reduce (rather than eliminate) its future commitment; or (iii) conditioning BFO's election on the GP's failure to secure LPAC approval of a replacement key person within the 180-day period.
The LPA imposes significant restrictions on the transferability of LP interests. The key transfer provisions are as follows:

Affiliate Transfer Exception. The LPA provides a limited exception for transfers to affiliates of the transferring LP. An LP may transfer all or a portion of its interest to an "affiliate" (as defined in the LPA) without GP consent, provided that: (i) the transferring LP provides the GP with at least 30 days' prior written notice of the proposed transfer, (ii) the GP's consent to the transfer is obtained (which consent may not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed), and (iii) the transferee affiliate executes a joinder agreement and becomes bound by all provisions of the LPA. We note that, while the LPA states that GP consent for affiliate transfers may not be "unreasonably withheld," this standard still provides the GP with meaningful discretion to block a proposed transfer on reasonable grounds.

BFO's concern is as follows: if the Anchor Investor carve-out is a blanket exclusion covering all terms (as the GP has proposed), then Anchor Investors could receive enhanced governance and transparency rights — such as LPAC seats, expanded consent rights, veto rights over certain fund actions, or enhanced reporting and information access — and those rights would be entirely excluded from the MFN. BFO would have no ability to elect to receive those same governance and transparency protections, regardless of BFO's own commitment size or the nature of the rights at issue.

2.  Draw the Governance/Transparency Distinction. BFO should then clearly articulate the distinction between economic terms and governance/transparency terms. Governance and transparency rights — including LPAC observer or voting seats, expanded consent rights, enhanced reporting timelines, ESG reporting, portfolio-level data access, and similar provisions — serve a fundamentally different function than economic concessions. They promote fund accountability, enable informed investor decision-making, and support the oversight framework contemplated by the LPA. Importantly, the extension of governance and transparency rights to additional limited partners does not impose a material cost on the GP or dilute the value of those rights for Anchor Investors. These rights are not zero-sum: an LPAC observer seat for BFO does not diminish the value of an LPAC voting seat held by an Anchor Investor.

•  Fallback: If the GP insists on a blanket carve-out covering both economic and governance terms, BFO can accept the blanket carve-out provided that enhanced reporting rights — specifically, quarterly and annual financial reporting timelines, ESG reporting obligations, and portfolio-level data access — are expressly excluded from the carve-out regardless of the committing LP's commitment level. Under this formulation, BFO would concede on LPAC seats, consent rights, and other governance provisions, but would preserve its core transparency and reporting objectives through a targeted carve-out to the carve-out.

The Fund IV LPA contains standard key person provisions, set forth in Section 9.4 of the LPA, identifying Conrad J. Ellsworth (Founder and Managing Partner of Meridian Peak Capital Advisors LLC) and Priya Narayan (Partner and Chief Investment Officer of Meridian Peak Capital Advisors LLC) as the Fund's designated key persons. Under the LPA, a "Key Person Event" occurs if either Ellsworth or Narayan ceases to devote substantially all of his or her professional time and attention to the affairs of the Fund, subject to customary exceptions for temporary absences, illness, and similar circumstances. Upon the occurrence of a Key Person Event, the LPA provides for a fund-level suspension of the investment period, during which the GP may not make new investments (other than follow-on investments and commitments to fund existing obligations), pending a vote of the LPAC or the advisory committee on whether to reinstate the investment period.

2.  Suspension vs. Notice Right. BFO should firmly resist the GP's attempt to recharacterize the right from a "suspension" to a mere "notice right." The distinction is substantive and consequential. Under a suspension, BFO's capital call obligations are tolled during the suspension period, and BFO is not exposed to default risk for declining to fund during that window. Under a notice right, capital calls continue to accrue and BFO must affirmatively elect within a compressed timeframe or lose the protection entirely. A suspension right provides BFO with the breathing room to conduct a meaningful assessment of successor leadership without the pressure of ongoing capital call obligations. This is consistent with the approach taken in the LPA itself: Section 9.4 of the LPA contemplates a fund-level suspension mechanism upon a Key Person Event, not merely a notice right. BFO's side-letter provision is designed to operate as a parallel individual right consistent with the fund-level architecture.

4.  Consistency with LPA Architecture. As noted above, the LPA's own key person provision in Section 9.4 contemplates a fund-level suspension mechanism. BFO's side-letter right is designed to operate in parallel with that fund-level protection, not to replace or supersede it. The side-letter provision merely allows BFO to exercise an individual right that is conceptually consistent with the collective right already embedded in the LPA. The GP should not object to affording BFO a right that mirrors a protection the GP has already agreed to at the fund level.

•  Preferred Outcome: 90-day suspension period, as proposed in BFO's initial draft. If the GP will agree to restore the 90-day period, BFO is willing to include a constructive cure provision as a concession: if the GP designates a successor key person who is approved by the LPAC within the 90-day suspension period, the suspension terminates automatically upon such approval, and BFO's capital call obligations resume in full without further action. This provision addresses the GP's concern about prolonged operational uncertainty while preserving BFO's right to a meaningful evaluation period.

First Close Timeline. Fund IV's anticipated first close is April 30, 2024. The final close deadline under the LPA is October 31, 2024. Specifically, the LP default consequences under the LPA include, among other remedies available to the GP: (i) forfeiture of a specified portion of the defaulting LP's partnership interest (the LPA provides for forfeiture of up to 50% of the defaulting LP's existing interest), (ii) loss of voting rights with respect to the defaulting LP's remaining interest, (iii) accrual of default interest on the unpaid amount at a rate of the lesser of 18% per annum or the maximum rate permitted by applicable law, and (iv) the GP's right to effect a forced transfer of the defaulting LP's interest to a third party on terms determined by the GP, without the defaulting LP's consent. The LPA provides for an initial capital call of 100% of each limited partner's total committed capital, to be funded at the closing of the acquisition. Accordingly, Pellegrino's entire $25,000,000 commitment will be called and must be funded on or before the closing date of January 30, 2026. The General Partner is required to provide no less than 10 business days' prior written notice of the capital call, together with wire instructions for the escrow account maintained by Continental Fiduciary Services, Inc. as the designated escrow agent.

The General Partner has the right, exercisable at its sole discretion, to extend the term of the Co-Invest Vehicle for up to two additional one-year periods. If both extension rights are exercised, the term would expire on January 30, 2038. The extension rights may be exercised sequentially, and no limited partner consent or advisory committee approval is required for the General Partner to exercise either extension.

Market Comparison. A 10-year initial term with two one-year extension periods is standard for private equity fund co-investment vehicles, which typically have initial terms ranging from 8 to 12 years with one to three extension periods. Some co-invest LPAs include a provision requiring LP advisory committee approval or consultation before extensions are exercised. The current LPA does not require LPAC approval for extensions, although the LPAC has a consultative role on the extension decision.

Recommendation. During the December 6, 2025 markup, we raised the issue of LP consent or LPAC approval for extensions. Ridgeline declined to include a consent or approval mechanism, citing the co-terminous structure with Fund IV as providing sufficient alignment of interests. In the January negotiation calls, Ridgeline's counsel confirmed, on the record, that the extension rights would only be exercised in connection with corresponding extensions of Fund IV's term, and that Ridgeline does not intend to extend the Co-Invest Vehicle independently of the main fund. This confirmation is documented in our negotiation record and in correspondence with Hartwell Velmoran & Pratt LLP, but it is not reflected in the LPA itself and therefore is not contractually binding. We consider this to be an acceptable risk given the co-terminous provision in the LPA, which provides a structural safeguard against independent extension of the Co-Invest Vehicle, and given the practical reality that an extension of the Co-Invest Vehicle without a corresponding extension of Fund IV would serve no commercial purpose.
A. Limited Partner Advisory Committee (LPAC)

The LPA establishes a three-member Limited Partner Advisory Committee (the "LPAC" or the "Advisory Committee"). The LPAC is composed of representatives of the Co-Invest Vehicle's limited partners, selected based on commitment size and investment profile.

Pursuant to Section 3.1 of the Side Letter, Pellegrino is entitled to one seat on the LPAC. The Pellegrino representative on the LPAC shall be designated by Pellegrino and may be replaced at any time upon written notice to the General Partner. The LPAC seat right is personal to Pellegrino and is not transferable with Pellegrino's limited partnership interest without the prior written consent of the General Partner.
The LPAC has a consultative role with respect to the following matters:
(d) Such other matters as the General Partner may refer to the LPAC from time to time.

It is important to note that the LPAC's role is consultative rather than approval-based. The General Partner is obligated to consult with the LPAC on the foregoing matters and to consider the LPAC's input in good faith, but the LPAC does not have the authority to approve, disapprove, or veto any action by the General Partner. The General Partner retains sole decision-making authority on all matters within its purview under the LPA.

The LPAC is required to meet at least annually. Additional meetings may be convened upon the request of any LPAC member or by the General Partner. Meetings may be held in person or by teleconference, and the General Partner is responsible for providing the LPAC with reasonable advance notice and supporting materials for each meeting.

Market Comparison. An LPAC seat for a co-investor holding a 33.33% interest in the vehicle is appropriate and consistent with market practice. In our experience, LPAC seats are typically offered to co-investors holding 25% or more of the vehicle's aggregate commitments. The consultative (rather than approval) authority is typical for co-invest vehicles, where the General Partner's ability to act quickly and decisively on behalf of the co-investors is an important structural feature.

As noted in Section IV above, extension of the Co-Invest Vehicle's term does not require limited partner consent under the final agreed form of the LPA; the LPAC has a consultative role only with respect to extensions.

The LPA imposes strict restrictions on the transfer, sale, assignment, pledge, or other disposition of limited partnership interests. No limited partner may transfer, sell, assign, pledge, hypothecate, or otherwise dispose of all or any portion of its limited partnership interest in the Co-Invest Vehicle without the prior written consent of the General Partner, which consent may be granted, conditioned, or withheld in the General Partner's sole and absolute discretion.

Recommendation. Pellegrino should be aware that there is no contractual mechanism to force a liquidity event. The LPAC seat secured through the Side Letter, combined with the monthly reporting rights described in Section VIII below and ongoing communication with the Ridgeline team, provides Pellegrino with informal influence on exit timing and strategy. We recommend that Pellegrino use the LPAC platform and the relationship with Connor Rafferty to stay actively engaged in exit planning discussions as they develop over the course of the hold period. The co-terminous term provision with Fund IV also provides assurance that exit timing will be driven by Fund IV's lifecycle, creating alignment between Pellegrino's exit expectations and the sponsor's fund-level considerations.

The LPA includes default provisions that impose significant penalties on any limited partner that fails to meet its capital call obligations. Given the structure of this co-investment — a single capital call at closing with no follow-on obligations — the default provisions have limited practical applicability but are worth understanding.

Market Comparison. The 50% forfeiture penalty is at the more punitive end of market practice. In our experience, default remedies in co-invest vehicles typically involve either (i) a forfeiture or dilution of 25% to 50% of the defaulting limited partner's interest, (ii) loss of voting rights and LPAC participation, or (iii) a combination of the foregoing. The 50% forfeiture rate is within the market range but at the high end. However, the practical significance of this provision is minimal in the context of Pellegrino's co-investment. Since 100% of committed capital is called at closing and there are no follow-on commitment obligations, the default provision would only be triggered if Pellegrino fails to fund the initial $25,000,000 closing capital call. If Pellegrino funds at closing — as expected — the default provision will never be invoked.

The Side Letter Agreement between the General Partner and Pellegrino contains a number of additional protective provisions beyond those set forth in the LPA. The Side Letter is binding on the General Partner and its successors and assigns, and the rights granted thereunder are in addition to (and not in limitation of) Pellegrino's rights under the LPA. The key Side Letter provisions are summarized below.
B. LPAC Seat

As described in Section V.A above, the Side Letter guarantees Pellegrino one seat on the three-member LPAC. This right is personal to Pellegrino and is not transferable with Pellegrino's limited partnership interest without the prior written consent of the General Partner.

Market Comparison. An LPAC seat for a co-investor holding a 33.33% interest in the vehicle is consistent with market practice. LPAC seats are typically offered to co-investors holding 25% or more of aggregate commitments.

FIRPTA. The Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act ("FIRPTA") imposes special withholding and tax obligations on dispositions of U.S. real property interests ("USRPIs") by foreign persons. While Pellegrino is a domestic entity and therefore not directly subject to FIRPTA withholding, the FIRPTA analysis is relevant to the extent that certain foreign co-investors in the vehicle may be affected, which could in turn affect the timing or mechanics of exit transactions. More importantly, the FIRPTA analysis is relevant to the characterization of the Co-Invest Vehicle's investment. Clarion's primary business is hotel management and asset management services, rather than direct ownership of U.S. real property. Based on the current business model, the Co-Invest Vehicle's interest in AcquisitionCo is not expected to constitute a USRPI. However, this conclusion is fact-dependent and could change if Clarion's business model shifts toward direct ownership of hotel real estate assets (as opposed to management of third-party-owned properties). Pellegrino should monitor this risk on an ongoing basis through the monthly reporting and LPAC participation.
LPAC Seat

Overall Assessment. The negotiated package of LPA terms and Side Letter protections is favorable for Pellegrino's position as a $25,000,000 co-investor. The economic terms — 10% carried interest, 8% preferred return compounded quarterly, and 0% management fee — are at or above market for sponsor-led co-invest vehicles. The governance and protective provisions — LPAC seat, dual Key Person trigger, full tag-along at both levels, full MFN, and no excuse/exclusion — are robust and provide Pellegrino with meaningful influence and protection throughout the life of the investment. The Side Letter provisions securing future hospitality co-investment allocation rights and enhanced reporting represent additional value beyond the standard co-invest package and reflect the strategic nature of the relationship between Pellegrino and Ridgeline.

4. LPAC Approval for Term Extensions. Pellegrino requested that the LPAC have approval authority (rather than merely consultative authority) over the General Partner's exercise of term extension rights. Ridgeline declined, citing the co-terminous structure with Fund IV as providing sufficient alignment and the need for the General Partner to have flexibility in managing the vehicle's term. The issue was resolved with the LPAC retaining consultative (but not approval) authority on extensions. Ridgeline confirmed verbally and in correspondence that extensions would only be exercised in connection with Fund IV extensions, although this commitment is not reflected in the LPA.

1.  Management Rollover Dilution. Monitor the management rollover structure (approximately $30,000,000 from Ted Barrington and Lisa Kwon) and its dilutive impact on Pellegrino's indirect ownership percentage of AcquisitionCo. The rollover equity is being structured through a separate Management Stockholders' Agreement, and any subsequent grants of management equity (including stock options, restricted stock, or profits interests) could further dilute Pellegrino's indirect ownership position. Pellegrino should request periodic updates on the capitalization table of AcquisitionCo through the LPAC.

3.  LPAC Participation and Monthly Reporting. Actively utilize the LPAC seat and the monthly reporting dashboards to maintain visibility into Clarion's operations, financial performance, and strategic initiatives. The LPAC seat provides an important platform for engaging with the General Partner on valuation, conflicts, exit planning, and other material matters.

•  The governance protections — including the LPAC seat, dual Key Person provision, full tag-along rights at both the vehicle and AcquisitionCo levels, full MFN protection, and the Side Letter prohibition on excuse/exclusion without Pellegrino's consent — are robust and provide Pellegrino with meaningful influence, transparency, and protection throughout the life of the investment.

•  The areas where Pellegrino's initial positions were not fully achieved — including the carried interest rate (10% vs. requested 0%), the Key Person trigger structure (dual vs. requested single), the absence of LPAC approval authority for extensions, and the absence of a separate cure period for defaults — represent reasonable compromises that are consistent with market practice and do not materially disadvantage Pellegrino's position.

**[MATTER CLOSING MEMORANDUM]{.underline}**

**[Matter No. 1026-00001]{.underline}**

**CALDERWOOD & HARKNESS LLP** 425 Lexington Avenue New York, NY 10017

**INTERNAL MEMORANDUM --- PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL**

This memorandum constitutes attorney work product and is protected by the attorney-client privilege and the work product doctrine. It is intended solely for internal use by the attorneys and professional staff of Calderwood & Harkness LLP involved in this matter. This memorandum should not be disclosed to any third party without the prior written consent of the Responsible Partner.

**Date:** April 5, 2024

**To:** File --- Matter No. 1026-00001

**From:** Pamela Cross, Responsible Partner, Funds & Asset Management

**Re:** Matter Closing Memorandum --- Briarwood Family Office LLC / Meridian Peak Capital Partners Fund IV, L.P. --- Side-Letter Negotiation

**Matter Number:** 1026-00001

**Status:** CLOSED --- TERMINATED

**[1. Purpose]{.underline}**

This memorandum documents the formal closing and termination of Matter No. 1026-00001 and is prepared in accordance with Calderwood & Harkness LLP\'s matter closing policies and procedures. The purpose of this memorandum is to create a comprehensive record of the work performed, the status of all documents and deliverables, the financial summary of the engagement, and the circumstances surrounding the termination of the matter, so that the firm\'s files may be properly closed and archived.

The matter involved the representation of Briarwood Family Office LLC (\"BFO\") in the negotiation of a side letter in connection with a proposed Seventy-Five Million Dollar (\$75,000,000) limited partnership commitment to Meridian Peak Capital Partners Fund IV, L.P. (\"Fund IV\" or the \"Fund\"), a Delaware limited partnership managed by Meridian Peak Capital Advisors LLC (\"MPCA\" or the \"Sponsor\"). Calderwood & Harkness LLP (\"C&H\" or the \"Firm\") was retained to review the Fund\'s offering and governing documents, advise BFO on the terms thereof, negotiate a side letter containing customized economic, governance, and reporting provisions on BFO\'s behalf, and review and mark up the subscription documents in anticipation of the commitment.

On April 2, 2024, BFO\'s investment committee reconvened and voted to decline the proposed commitment to Fund IV. On April 3, 2024, Sandra M. Whitfield, General Counsel of BFO, notified the undersigned of BFO\'s decision and instructed C&H to transmit a formal withdrawal letter to counsel for the Fund\'s general partner and to the Sponsor. On April 4, 2024, the undersigned transmitted such withdrawal letter, confirming that all draft side-letter provisions had lapsed without execution, that no subscription agreement had been executed, and that no capital commitment had been made by BFO to Fund IV.

As a consequence of BFO\'s decision, all draft side-letter provisions --- including, without limitation, the most favored nation rights, excuse and exclusion rights, management fee concessions, co-investment rights, enhanced reporting obligations, key person enhancements, transfer rights, confidentiality carve-outs, tax reporting commitments, and placement fee offset provisions that had been the subject of negotiation over the preceding approximately ten weeks --- lapsed and are of no further force or effect. No subscription agreement was executed, and no capital commitment of any kind was made by BFO to Fund IV or to any affiliated vehicle.

This matter is hereby closed effective as of the date hereof.

**[2. Client Information]{.underline}**

**Client:** Briarwood Family Office LLC

**Entity Type:** Delaware limited liability company

**Principal Business Address:** 780 Park Avenue, Suite 3200, New York, NY 10021

**Registered Agent:** Capitol Registered Agents Inc., 1209 Orange Street, Wilmington, Delaware 19801

**Employer Identification Number (EIN):** 27-4831956

**Assets Under Management:** Approximately \$1.8 billion (as of December 31, 2023, per information provided by BFO)

**Primary Contacts:**

> • **Julian R. Hargrove** --- Managing Director & Chief Investment Officer. Mr. Hargrove serves as the principal decision-maker for BFO\'s investment activities and holds a veto right over all investment committee determinations. He was the ultimate authority on the proposed commitment to Fund IV and participated in strategic discussions regarding the scope and priority of side-letter negotiations.
>
> • **Sandra M. Whitfield** --- General Counsel. Ms. Whitfield served as BFO\'s primary point of contact with C&H throughout the engagement. She executed the engagement letter on behalf of BFO on January 24, 2024, and communicated BFO\'s instructions, feedback, and ultimate decision to decline the commitment. All formal communications between C&H and BFO were directed through Ms. Whitfield.
>
> • **Derek T. Calloway** --- Director of External Investments. Mr. Calloway was responsible for BFO\'s evaluation of the Fund IV opportunity from an investment and due diligence perspective. He participated in the four-party conference call on March 11, 2024 and provided input on the commercial terms of the side letter, including fee economics and co-investment structuring.
>
> • **Renata Vasquez** --- Investment Analyst. Ms. Vasquez supported Mr. Calloway in the due diligence process and served as a secondary contact for document production and information requests.

**Client Background:** BFO is a single-family office established in 2007 for the purpose of managing the wealth of the Hargrove family. The Hargrove family\'s wealth was principally derived from commercial real estate development activities in the northeastern United States, including the development and management of office, mixed-use, and multifamily properties across the greater New York metropolitan area and New England. BFO\'s investment strategy encompasses four primary verticals: (i) direct real estate investments, (ii) real estate credit strategies, (iii) private equity, and (iv) liquid alternatives. BFO typically allocates between fifteen percent (15%) and twenty percent (20%) of its total assets under management to third-party managed funds, with a preference for commingled vehicles managed by established sponsors with demonstrated track records. The proposed commitment to Fund IV fell within this allocation strategy and was consistent with BFO\'s historical appetite for institutional-quality real estate private equity vehicles.

**Firm Overview:** MPCA was founded in 2011 and operates as a mid-market private equity firm focused on value-add and opportunistic real estate investments, real estate operating companies, and asset-management platform acquisitions across North America. Since its founding, MPCA has raised and managed three prior funds (Meridian Peak Capital Partners Fund I, L.P.; Meridian Peak Capital Partners Fund II, L.P.; and Meridian Peak Capital Partners Fund III, L.P.), which in the aggregate have attracted approximately \$3.2 billion in limited partner commitments. MPCA\'s investment team is based primarily in Boston, with additional professionals in New York and Los Angeles. Mr. Ellsworth and Ms. Narayan serve as the key persons for Fund IV, and their continued involvement was a significant focus of the side-letter negotiation as described in Section 5.2 of this memorandum.

The General Partner has no independent operations, employees, or assets apart from its interest in Fund IV.

**[3.3 The Fund]{.underline}**

**5.2.1 Proposed Side-Letter Terms (as Negotiated but Never Executed)**

The following is a comprehensive summary of the side-letter terms that were the subject of negotiation between C&H (on behalf of BFO) and Ashford Crane & Hewitt LLP (on behalf of the GP). It is emphasized that all of the terms described below were contained in draft documents only, were the subject of ongoing negotiation, and lapsed without execution upon BFO\'s decision to decline the commitment. No side letter was ever executed, and none of the provisions described below have any legal force or effect.

**Most Favored Nation (\"MFN\") Rights:**

> BFO was to be entitled to elect any economic or governance term granted to any other limited partner committing Fifty Million Dollars (\$50,000,000) or more to Fund IV. The MFN right was subject to the following carve-outs:
>
> • **Anchor Investor Carve-Out:** Terms granted exclusively to limited partners committing Two Hundred Million Dollars (\$200,000,000) or more (representing 13.33% of the Fund\'s target size of \$1.5 billion) would be excluded from the MFN universe. This threshold was agreed during the four-party conference call on March 11, 2024.
>
> • **Regulatory Accommodations:** Terms granted to limited partners solely to accommodate regulatory requirements applicable to ERISA plans, tax-exempt entities, or governmental plans would be excluded from the MFN universe.
>
> • **GP Affiliates:** Terms granted to affiliates of the General Partner or MPCA would be excluded from the MFN universe.
>
> The General Partner was to deliver a redacted summary of all material side-letter terms to BFO within fifteen (15) business days of the applicable closing at which such side letters were entered into. BFO would then have a period of twenty (20) business days following receipt of such summary to elect to adopt any available MFN terms. (Note: The timing of the GP\'s delivery obligation --- 15 versus 20 business days --- remained a bracketed open point as of the last draft exchanged.)

**Excuse and Exclusion Rights:**

> BFO was to have the right to be excused from, or excluded from, participation in certain categories of investments. The excusable investment categories agreed upon by the parties were:
>
> • Cannabis-related assets (including any investment in a portfolio company deriving more than a de minimis portion of its revenue from the cultivation, processing, distribution, or sale of cannabis or cannabis-related products);
>
> • Gaming and casino properties;
>
> • Investments located in, or involving counterparties domiciled in, jurisdictions subject to comprehensive U.S. sanctions administered by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (\"OFAC\"); and
>
> • Investments that would cause BFO to hold \"plan assets\" within the meaning of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, as amended (\"ERISA\"), and the regulations promulgated thereunder.
>
> The excuse right was to be exercisable by BFO within fifteen (15) business days of receipt of a capital call notice or investment notice describing the proposed investment.
>
> The aggregate excuse cap --- representing the maximum cumulative amount of capital calls from which BFO could be excused --- was a significant point of dispute that remained unresolved at the time of termination. The General Partner\'s position was that the excuse cap should be set at twenty percent (20%) of BFO\'s commitment, or \$15,000,000. C&H, on behalf of BFO, counter-proposed an excuse cap of twenty-five percent (25%) of BFO\'s commitment, or \$18,750,000. The Excuse Rights Analysis Memorandum delivered to BFO on March 6, 2024 recommended maintaining the 25% position, with a fallback authorization to accept a 20% cap if necessary to reach agreement on the overall package of terms.

**Management Fee Reduction:**

> BFO was to receive a reduced management fee as follows:
>
> • **During the Investment Period:** 1.50% per annum on committed capital (versus the standard LPA rate of 1.75% per annum on committed capital), representing a reduction of 25 basis points.
>
> • **Post-Investment Period:** 1.25% per annum on invested capital (versus the standard LPA rate of 1.50% per annum on invested capital), representing a reduction of 25 basis points.
>
> Based on BFO\'s proposed \$75,000,000 commitment and the applicable fee bases, the estimated annual savings during the four-year investment period would have been approximately \$187,500 per year (i.e., 0.25% × \$75,000,000), for cumulative savings of approximately \$750,000 over the full investment period. Post-investment period savings would have varied based on the level of invested capital at the applicable measurement dates.

**[C. Economics]{.underline}**

The economic terms of the Vehicle have been negotiated to reflect the co-investment nature of the arrangement and are significantly more favorable to Ironside than the standard economic terms applicable to Fund IV\'s main limited partnership. The key economic terms are summarized below:

**Management Fee.** No management fee (0%) is charged on the Vehicle. This is a material economic benefit to Ironside, as Fund IV\'s main limited partnership is subject to a management fee of 2% per annum on committed capital during the investment period and 2% per annum on invested capital thereafter.

**Carried Interest.** The General Partner is entitled to a carried interest of 10% of net profits above the preferred return, as compared to the 20% carried interest applicable in Fund IV\'s main limited partnership. The reduced carried interest rate reflects the co-investment nature of the Vehicle and Ironside\'s significant capital commitment. The carried interest is subject to the distribution waterfall mechanics described in Section XI of this memorandum.

**Preferred Return.** The Limited Partner and the General Partner are entitled to a preferred return of 8% per annum, compounded quarterly, on their respective contributed capital. The preferred return must be satisfied in full before any carried interest is payable to the General Partner.

**GP Commitment.** The General Partner has committed \$30,000 (0.01% of total committed capital) as its capital contribution to the Partnership. While the GP commitment is modest in absolute terms, it is typical for co-investment vehicles where the sponsor\'s primary capital commitment is made through the main fund.

**[D. Purpose]{.underline}**

The sole purpose of the Partnership, as set forth in Section 2.01 of the LP Agreement, is to co-invest alongside Fund IV in the acquisition of 100% of the outstanding equity interests of Cascadia Renewables Holdings, Inc. through Cascadia Acquisition Corp., a Delaware corporation to be formed as the acquisition subsidiary. Cascadia Acquisition Corp. will be wholly owned, directly or indirectly, by Fund IV and the Vehicle in proportion to their respective equity commitments (71.43% Fund IV / 28.57% Vehicle).

The Vehicle\'s co-investment percentage of total equity is 28.57%, calculated as \$300,000,000 divided by \$1,050,000,000 in total equity commitments. The Co-Investment Allocation Agreement governs the allocation mechanics and ensures parallel treatment of Fund IV and the Vehicle throughout the life of the investment.

The Partnership is not authorized to engage in any business or activity other than the foregoing, and the General Partner is not authorized to cause the Partnership to make any investment other than the Cascadia co-investment without the prior written consent of the Limited Partner.

These consent requirements are designed to protect Ironside\'s interests as the sole limited partner and to ensure that the General Partner does not take any material action that could adversely affect Ironside\'s investment without Ironside\'s knowledge and approval. **[C. LP Advisory Committee]{.underline}**

No formal Limited Partner Advisory Committee (\"LPAC\") is established under the LP Agreement. The absence of a formal LPAC is appropriate given the single-LP structure of the Vehicle --- there is no need for a committee to represent the interests of multiple limited partners, as Ironside is the sole limited partner and has direct consent rights on all material matters.

In lieu of a formal LPAC, the Side Letter provides for direct consultation between the General Partner and Ironside on material matters affecting the Partnership and its investment. The GP has agreed to consult with Ironside in good faith on matters that would customarily be brought before an LPAC in a multi-investor fund, including conflict-of-interest matters, related-party transactions, valuation issues, and material deviations from the investment thesis.

**[D. Investment Decisions]{.underline}**

All investment decisions relating to the Partnership\'s investment in Cascadia are made by the General Partner in its sole discretion, subject to the limitations described in Section IV.B above. This includes decisions relating to the initial acquisition of Cascadia, any post-closing add-on investments or capital expenditures at the portfolio-company level, any restructuring, recapitalization, or refinancing of Cascadia, and any ultimate disposition or exit of the investment.

The Co-Investment Allocation Agreement governs the parallel investment mechanics between Fund IV and the Vehicle, ensuring that both entities participate in the acquisition and all subsequent investment decisions on a pro rata basis (28.57% Vehicle / 71.43% Fund IV). The Co-Investment Allocation Agreement provides for parallel economic treatment, meaning that Fund IV and the Vehicle receive the same terms with respect to the acquisition, any subsequent investments, and the ultimate disposition of the investment, subject to differences in their respective economic terms (e.g., the Vehicle\'s lower carried interest rate).

Any deviation from the pro rata allocation set forth in the Co-Investment Allocation Agreement requires the prior written consent of the Limited Partner (Ironside). This provision protects Ironside against dilution or adverse reallocation of investment economics as between Fund IV and the Vehicle.

**[V. Fiduciary Duties]{.underline}**

**[A. Standard of Care]{.underline}**

Under the LP Agreement, the General Partner owes fiduciary duties to the Partnership and its partners. These duties are, however, subject to the modifications and limitations permitted under the Delaware Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act, which provides substantial flexibility to the parties to a limited partnership agreement to define and modify the fiduciary duties owed by the general partner.

The LP Agreement modifies the default fiduciary duties as follows:

**Duty of Care.** The duty of care owed by the General Partner is limited to a \"gross negligence or willful misconduct\" standard. Under this standard, the General Partner is not liable to the Partnership or any partner for errors in judgment, losses, or other adverse outcomes arising from its management of the Partnership\'s affairs, unless such errors, losses, or outcomes result from the General Partner\'s gross negligence, willful misconduct, fraud, or bad faith. This modification is consistent with the standard of care commonly adopted in Delaware limited partnership agreements for private equity and infrastructure funds and is permissible under DRULPA Section 17-1101(d).

**Duty of Loyalty.** The duty of loyalty owed by the General Partner is preserved but is qualified to account for the General Partner\'s role as the sponsor of Fund IV and other investment vehicles. Specifically, the LP Agreement provides that the General Partner and its affiliates (including Meridian and Fund IV) may engage in other business activities, including activities that compete with or are similar to the Partnership\'s business, without any obligation to account to the Partnership for any profits or benefits derived from such activities. This qualification is necessary to accommodate the General Partner\'s role as the general partner of Fund IV and its other investment activities, and the specific allocation as between Fund IV and the Vehicle is governed by the Co-Investment Allocation Agreement.

**[B. Exculpation]{.underline}**

The LP Agreement includes a customary exculpation provision that limits the personal liability of the General Partner and certain related persons in connection with the Partnership\'s activities. Specifically, the General Partner and its affiliates, managers, members, officers, and employees (collectively, the \"Covered Persons\") are exculpated from liability to the Partnership or the Limited Partner for any act or omission taken or suffered in good faith and reasonably believed by the applicable Covered Person to be within the scope of the authority conferred by the LP Agreement, except to the extent that such act or omission constitutes gross negligence, willful misconduct, fraud, or bad faith.

The exculpation provision is drafted broadly to cover the full range of activities that the Covered Persons may undertake in connection with the Partnership\'s business, including investment decisions, operational decisions, service provider engagement, and all other actions taken in the course of managing the Partnership\'s affairs. The carve-outs for gross negligence, willful misconduct, fraud, and bad faith ensure that the Covered Persons remain accountable for egregious conduct while providing appropriate protection against liability for good-faith errors in judgment.

**[C. Indemnification]{.underline}**

The LP Agreement provides for indemnification of the Covered Persons by the Partnership against losses, damages, liabilities, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys\' fees and expenses) arising out of or in connection with the Partnership\'s activities. The indemnification obligation is subject to the same carve-outs applicable to the exculpation provision --- indemnification is not available to the extent that the conduct giving rise to the claim constitutes gross negligence, willful misconduct, fraud, or bad faith.

Several important features of the indemnification provision merit emphasis:

> • The indemnification obligations of the Partnership are payable solely from Partnership assets. The Limited Partner has no personal obligation to fund indemnification payments, and the General Partner may not issue capital calls specifically to fund indemnification obligations without the Limited Partner\'s consent.
>
> • The LP Agreement permits advancement of expenses (including attorneys\' fees) to Covered Persons in connection with pending or threatened proceedings, subject to an undertaking by the applicable Covered Person to repay such amounts if it is ultimately determined that indemnification is not available under the terms of the LP Agreement.
>
> • The indemnification provision is not exclusive and does not preclude any Covered Person from seeking indemnification or contribution from any other source, including insurance policies maintained by the General Partner or its affiliates.

**[D. Delaware Law Considerations]{.underline}**

The fiduciary duty, exculpation, and indemnification provisions of the LP Agreement have been drafted in accordance with the requirements and limitations of DRULPA. Several provisions of DRULPA are particularly relevant:

**DRULPA § 17-1101(d).** This section provides that a limited partnership agreement may modify, restrict, or expand the fiduciary duties owed by a partner or other person to the partnership or to another partner. The statute expressly permits the elimination of fiduciary duties, subject to the limitation that a partnership agreement may not eliminate the implied contractual covenant of good faith and fair dealing.

**Implied Covenant of Good Faith and Fair Dealing.** In accordance with DRULPA Section 17-1101(d), the LP Agreement expressly preserves the implied contractual covenant of good faith and fair dealing. This covenant provides a baseline level of protection for the Limited Partner against arbitrary or opportunistic conduct by the General Partner, even in areas where the LP Agreement has modified or limited the General Partner\'s fiduciary duties. Delaware courts have consistently held that the implied covenant serves as a gap-filling mechanism to address situations not expressly covered by the partnership agreement, and the preservation of this covenant in the LP Agreement is both appropriate and consistent with best practices.

The modifications to default fiduciary duties set forth in the LP Agreement are within the range of market practice for Delaware limited partnerships in the private equity and infrastructure asset classes and have been reviewed and approved by the Responsible Partner.
